questions.question_text:
A population has $\mu=84$ and $\sigma=21$.
Samples of size $49$ are taken.
Find $E(\bar{X})$ and $\mathrm{sd}(\bar{X})$.

options.why: Divided $\sigma$ by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.
Divided the mean by $\sqrt{n}$ as well; the centre of the sampling distribution stays at $\mu$.
Divided the mean by $\sqrt{n}$ and divided $\sigma$ by $n$ rather than $\sqrt{n}$.

questions.question_text:
A population has $\sigma=9$.
Samples of size $27$ are taken.
Find $\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X})$.

options.why: Gave the standard deviation $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ instead of the variance.
Divided $\sigma$ by $n$ without squaring $\sigma$ first.
Squared $\sigma$ but divided by $\sqrt{n}$ instead of by $n$.

questions.question_text: By what factor must a sample size be multiplied so that the standard error of the mean is halved?

options.why: Treats the standard error as inversely proportional to $n$, but it is inversely proportional to $\sqrt{n}$.
Took the square root of the halving factor instead of squaring it.
Applied the squaring twice, giving $2^{4}$ instead of $2^{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
$\mathrm{sd}(\bar{X})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$
Halving it requires $\sqrt{n}$ to double.
$(\text{new }n)=(2\sqrt{n})^{2}$
$=4n$
The sample size must be multiplied by $4$.

questions.question_text:
A population has $\sigma=30$.
Find the smallest sample size for which the standard error of the mean is at most $2$.

options.why: Solved $\frac{\sigma}{n}\le 2$, dividing by $n$ rather than by $\sqrt{n}$.
Set the variance $\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}$ to be at most $2$ instead of the standard deviation.
Multiplied $\sigma$ by $2$ instead of solving the inequality for $n$.

questions.question_text:
Samples of size $64$ from a population give a standard error of the mean of $1.6$.
Find the population standard deviation $\sigma$.

options.why: Multiplied by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.
Divided by $\sqrt{n}$ instead of multiplying, applying the formula the wrong way round.
Divided by $n$ instead of multiplying by $\sqrt{n}$.

questions.question_text:
The masses of packets of rice have $\mu=2.5$ kg and $\sigma=0.6$ kg.
Samples of $100$ packets are taken.
Find $E(\bar{X})$ and $\mathrm{sd}(\bar{X})$.

options.why: Divided $\sigma$ by $n$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}$.
Divided the mean by $\sqrt{n}$ as well; only the spread shrinks.
Divided the mean by $\sqrt{n}$ and divided $\sigma$ by $n$ rather than $\sqrt{n}$.

questions.question_text:
Samples of size $80$ from a population give $\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X})=0.45$.
Find the population standard deviation $\sigma$.

options.why: Stopped at the population variance without taking the square root.
Divided by $n$ instead of multiplying by $n$ before taking the square root.
Divided by $n$ instead of multiplying, and did not take the square root.

questions.question_text:
Machine A produces items whose lengths have $\sigma=7.5$ mm, and samples of $9$ items are taken.
Machine B is sampled in groups of $25$ items, and the standard error of the mean for machine B equals that for machine A.
Find the population standard deviation of machine B's lengths.

options.why: Gave the shared standard error rather than machine B's population standard deviation.
Multiplied the standard error by $n=25$ instead of by $\sqrt{n}=5$.
Scaled $7.5$ by $\frac{3}{5}$, inverting the ratio $\frac{\sqrt{25}}{\sqrt{9}}$ that is actually needed.

questions.solution_text:
For machine A, $\mathrm{sd}(\bar{X})=\frac{7.5}{\sqrt{9}}$
$=\frac{7.5}{3}$
$=2.5$
For machine B, $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{25}}=2.5$
$\frac{\sigma}{5}=2.5$
$\sigma=12.5$

questions.question_text:
Let $X\sim N(20,100)$.
Which event has the highest probability?

options.text: A value of $X$ is chosen at random and it is between 19 and 21
options.why: A single observation has the widest normal variability.

options.text: 5 values of $X$ are chosen at random and their mean is between 19 and 21
options.why: The five-value sample mean is less variable than X but more variable than the ten-value mean.

options.text: 10 values of $X$ are chosen at random and their mean is between 19 and 21
5 values of $X$ are chosen at random and they are all between 19 and 21
options.why: Requires every individual observation to fall in a narrow interval.

questions.solution_text: Here $\sigma=10$. For a sample mean of size $n$, the standard deviation is $10/\sqrt n$. The ten-value mean has the smaller standard error, $10/\sqrt{10}$, so it is most concentrated around the mean 20 and has the greatest probability of lying between 19 and 21.

questions.question_text: If $X\sim N(20,100)$, then the distribution of sample means of size $4$, $\bar X_4$, has...

options.why: Uses the original population variance without reducing it for averaging four observations.
Divides the variance by an incorrect factor rather than by the sample size $4$.
Halves the variance instead of applying the sampling-mean variance formula.

questions.solution_text: For a sample mean of size $n$, $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_4)=100/4=25$.
